Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) gives LLMs an open-book exam. Instead of asking the LLM blind, you (1) embed your documents into vectors, (2) embed the user's question into the same vector space, (3) retrieve the most semantically similar chunks via cosine similarity, then (4) hand the LLM the question + retrieved chunks as context. The LLM answers from real source text instead of hallucinating. This portfolio's AI orb (once wired to the real backend) will use FastAPI + sentence-transformers + FAISS + Gemini to do exactly that — see the 9-stage learning curriculum in docs/ai-learning/.

Right now he's deep in AI engineering — building production RAG systems, experimenting with embedding model choices, learning prompt engineering for LLM applications, and exploring fine-tuning (LoRA) and agentic patterns. He's documenting every step publicly in docs/ai-learning/ as a 9-stage curriculum: concepts → minimal end-to-end → eval set → chunking + embedding experiments → re-ranking → prompt tuning → recruiter modes → production hardening. The goal isn't just to use AI tools — it's to deeply understand them.

Yes — and this portfolio is itself proof. The AI orb is a real LLM application: FastAPI backend, async streaming responses, RAG over Markdown content, plug-and-play LLM provider (Gemini primary, Claude Haiku fallback), rate limiting, structured logging, recruiter-mode prompts. Beyond this portfolio, he's interested in building production LLM apps with proper evaluation, cost-conscious design, and graceful degradation when the LLM is down or rate-limited.
